You are role-playing a specific persona for a usability test. Stay fully in character.

PERSONA: You are an experienced professional software engineer, evaluating a new developer tool/pack called "live-spec" to decide whether it's worth a deeper look for your team. You know git, CLIs, regexes, config files, CI, etc. fluently. You are busy — you skim for signal, you want the fast path to technical substance, and you get irritated by marketing fluff that makes you hunt for the actual mechanics. You also don't want to be forced to read a huge wall of consumer-facing prose just to find the one technical fact you need.

TASK: Start by reading this file top to bottom: /private/tmp/live-spec-readme2/wt/README.md
This lives inside a git repo at /private/tmp/live-spec-readme2/wt — you may use Read/Grep/Glob/Bash(read-only) to open any file the README points you to (relative links, mentioned paths) to check that they exist and say what the README implies they say, the way a real engineer would click through. Do not run any script that writes/installs anything; read-only exploration only.

As you read, record a numbered list of "stumbles": anything that confuses you, wastes your time, feels evasive or marketing-fluffy where you wanted a fact, any link that points at a file that doesn't exist or doesn't contain what's implied, any internal contradiction, or anywhere you'd genuinely give up evaluating the tool. Also specifically evaluate: (a) is there a clear, fast, well-marked path from the top of the README to the real technical detail (config schema, the exact commands, script internals, hook wiring, CI wiring) without having to wade through customer-facing narrative? (b) does the document ever waste your time by making you read something before telling you it wasn't for you? For each stumble, quote the exact sentence/phrase and name the section heading it's under.

At the end, classify each stumble as BLOCKING (you'd stop evaluating / lose confidence in the project) or MINOR (mildly annoying but you'd continue). Give a final count: "N blocking, M minor." If the document actually serves you well end to end, say so plainly.

Report back your full numbered stumble list and the final blocking/minor count. Keep your response focused on the list — no preamble.

1	# live-spec
2	
3	**Ten working [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) skills, plus the one shared rulebook they all load. They turn a wish spoken in passing into a specified, reviewed, tested, committed change. Scripts block the push when the documents and the code disagree.**
4	
5	---
6	
7	You tell your agent *"the report page needs a date filter"* and four minutes later it is written, tested, and green. The tests pass because they came from the same spec. The spec never said what happens when the date is invalid, so the agent picked some behaviour and shipped it. Nobody chose that behaviour and nobody reviewed it, and the green suite never looked at it.
8	
9	That is the gap. The spec became the thing your agent builds from, and nothing checks the spec itself.
10	
11	live-spec closes it. You say the sentence in passing, with nothing to file and no form. It gets classified, written into a living spec, reviewed by a formal-verification pass, covered by tests derived from that spec, coded until green, and committed with its documents in one change. A script on the pre-push hook compares the spec to the code that shipped and refuses the push when the two disagree. There is no CLI. You talk to it.
12	
13	---
14	
15	## Install
16	
17	There are two ways in. Pick one road at step 1, then follow that road's lines wherever the steps below fork. Take the plugin road if you want to use the pack and download nothing you have to keep. Take the clone road if you want the pack's own tree on your disk, to read and to keep.
18	
19	### Step 1 — get the pack onto your machine
20	
21	**The plugin road.** Type two lines into Claude Code:
22	
23	```
24	/plugin marketplace add happysasha18/live-spec
25	/plugin install live-spec@live-spec
26	```
27	
28	That is the whole step. The plugin puts the entire pack tree under `~/.claude/plugins/cache/`. You do not clone this repository, now or later.
29	
30	**The clone road.** Clone the repository and run its installer:
31	
32	```
33	git clone https://github.com/happysasha18/live-spec.git
34	cd live-spec && ./install.sh
35	```
36	
37	`install.sh` copies the skill folders into `~/.claude/skills/` and copies nothing else. Keep the clone. It is your copy of the pack tree, and step 3 runs a script that lives inside it.
38	
39	### Step 2 — attach the pack to a project
40	
41	Both roads do the same thing here. Open the project in Claude Code and say *"attach live-spec to this project"*, or *"found a new project on live-spec"* in an empty directory. The pack locates its own tree and reads yours, asks what it needs to know in plain words, and runs the whole setup walk itself — writing your first spec, and (step 3, next) wiring the push gate. You do not open any of those files yourself.
42	
43	### Step 3 — the push gate
44	
45	The push gate is a separate step, and it reads the documents step 2 just wrote. **The setup walk installs it too, as part of the one walk from step 2** — the checks, the config, the git hook, all of it. That is the ordinary path, and there is nothing to do here.
46	
47	After that everything runs in plain words: any wish, *"status"* — where the work stands now and what is next — *"publish"*.
48	
49	If you're a programmer and want to read or drive those documents yourself, the technical account starts at ["For builders"](#for-builders), below the fold. A technical wish for the pack itself is welcome — [open an Issue](https://github.com/happysasha18/live-spec/issues/new/choose); it lands in the maintainers' inbox and gets routed from there.
50	
51	---
52	
53	## For builders
54	
55	Everything above is the whole job for a customer. What follows is for a programmer who wants to see what the setup walk does, run a piece of it by hand, wire the gate into CI, or drive the documents directly instead of through the agent.
56	
57	### The technical walk-throughs
58	
59	[`docs/adoption.md`](docs/adoption.md) explains the setup walk step 2 runs. The normative procedures it follows are [`adopt/ADOPT.md`](adopt/ADOPT.md) for an existing codebase and [`adopt/START.md`](adopt/START.md) for an empty directory.
60	
61	### The push gate, by hand
62	
63	Three things have to be true before any of it works, and each has one command that says so. `python3 --version` must print 3.9 or newer; install a newer Python if it does not. `git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree` must print `true` in your project's root; run `git init` there if it does not. And `git rev-parse --verify origin/main` must name a commit. The tests-present check diffs your work against that ref. If the command fails, you name your own base in the config instead, two paragraphs down. It fails on a project with no remote, and on one whose default branch is named otherwise. All of this assumes Claude Code on your machine: the pack is a set of skills it loads, and step 2 happens inside it.
64	
65	By hand, run one script from your project's root. It lives in the pack tree you already got in step 1, so the line you type depends on which road you took:
66	
67	```
68	# plugin road — the tree sits in the plugin cache
69	bash ~/.claude/plugins/cache/*/live-spec/*/adopt/install-scaffold.sh
70	
71	# clone road — the tree is the clone from step 1
72	bash /path/to/live-spec/adopt/install-scaffold.sh
73	```
74	
75	It writes six files into your project's `guardrails/`: the four checks, the shared library they load, and a copy of the page that documents them. It seeds `guardrails.config.json` when your project carries none, and it never overwrites a config you already filled. It also writes `scripts/ratchet-manifest.json`, creating a `scripts/` folder if you have none. A good run prints one `vendored:` line per file and a `seeded:` line for the config. Then it prints the manual steps that remain, and ends on a line reading `{"severity": "ok", "code": "scaffold-install", ...}`.
76	
77	That config then needs two things from you. Fill in your paths: the spec, the test matrix, the queue, the tests, and the surface registry. The registry is the table listing every surface the project ships. A surface is one named part a user meets: a screen, a page, a command, a public function. The queue is the dated list of what has been asked of the product and where each ask stands. This repository keeps its own in [`ROADMAP.md`](ROADMAP.md).
78	
79	Three more fields in that same config decide what the checks can see. The seeded example fills them with values a fresh project rarely matches. `user_facing_globs` names the files whose change demands a test. `rendered_artifacts`, or `render_command` instead, names what the completeness check reads as your shipped output. `surface_discovery_pattern` is the expression that finds surface ids inside that output. Leave the first two as they ship and two of the four checks go red on a path that does not exist. Leave the pattern matching nothing your artifacts contain and the check passes while seeing nothing. That is the one failure that never announces itself. The setup walk in step 2 fills this config for you from what your project ships; this paragraph is for a programmer editing it by hand instead.
80	
81	One field more, `base_ref`, decides what the tests-present check compares your work against when `origin/main` does not resolve. That means a project with no remote, or one whose default branch is named otherwise. Set it to your own base branch, `"base_ref": "main"`, and that check has its ground. Leave it out on such a project and the fourth line of the push gate reds with `no base ref to diff against`. [`scaffold/guardrails/README.md`](scaffold/guardrails/README.md) describes every field one at a time.
82	
83	Second, empty the config's `waivers` block, so the line reads `"waivers": {}`. It ships holding one example waiver, and that example switches the completeness check off. Every run prints `WAIVED (completeness): no rendered artifact yet — declared 2026-07-10, owner <maintainer>` and exits zero. The line is loud enough. What it says is that someone else's declaration, dated before you arrived, stands where your own would go. Until you empty the block, you run on three checks instead of four.
84	
85	One more step, outside the config: add these four lines to `.git/hooks/pre-push`.
86	
87	```sh
88	python3 guardrails/check_completeness.py || exit 1
89	python3 guardrails/check_tests_present.py || exit 1
90	python3 guardrails/check_traces_to_spec.py || exit 1
91	python3 guardrails/check_conflicts.py || exit 1
92	```
93	
94	Create that file if your project has none, and make it executable with `chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-push`. Run it once by hand with `sh .git/hooks/pre-push`, then `echo $?` to see the exit code. Four lines each opening `OK (` and a `0` mean the gate is live. The same four lines are in your own `guardrails/README.md`, the copy the script just vendored, on either road. Those hook lines take no arguments, so the `--base <ref>` flag the checks accept is for running one by hand. What the hook itself reads is `origin/main`, or the `base_ref` you set in the config. The setup walk writes this same hook file for you; this step is for a programmer who would rather write it themselves, or wire it into CI instead of `.git/hooks/`.
95	
96	Two more installers finish the gate the adoption procedure asks for. Both run from your project's root, out of the same pack tree as before:
97	
98	```
99	# plugin road
100	bash ~/.claude/plugins/cache/*/live-spec/*/adopt/install-ratchet.sh
101	bash ~/.claude/plugins/cache/*/live-spec/*/scripts/install-pack-hooks.sh
102	
103	# clone road
104	bash /path/to/live-spec/adopt/install-ratchet.sh
105	bash /path/to/live-spec/scripts/install-pack-hooks.sh
106	```
107	
108	The first vendors the style, redundancy, and freeze gates. It measures your documents as they stand today and writes the debt caps at those numbers. It generates `tests/test_ratchet_lock.py`, so the gate is green the day it lands and the debt can only hold or shrink from there. It ends by printing a fifth gate line for your push hook. That line belongs in the same `.git/hooks/pre-push` you just wrote, beside the four. Write it as `python3 -m pytest -q tests/test_ratchet_lock.py || exit 1`. The printed form ends `|| fail=1`, which fits a hook that collects every failure before it exits. The recipe labels it `gate r`. This repository's own hook set already gives that letter to a different check, so give yours another label if you carry that set.
109	
110	The second puts the pack's own scan hooks on your machine, and this one reaches outside your project. It copies the hook files under `~/.claude/hooks/` and writes their wiring into `~/.claude/settings.json`, which every project of yours reads. Run it with `--dry-run` first: it prints every file and every line it would add, and touches nothing. Running it for real twice changes nothing, and your personal overlay files are never written by it. [`adopt/ADOPT.md`](adopt/ADOPT.md) counts both installers as part of the attach. The setup walk runs both of these for you too; they are here for a programmer setting a project up outside a live-spec session.
111	
112	---
113	
114	## What the spec looks like
115	
116	A project under the pack keeps one document, `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, stating what the product promises today. A stranger can read a section on the first pass. The format is a requirements genre, defined in [`docs/spec-format.md`](docs/spec-format.md):
117	
118	- The document opens with a **glossary**. Every domain noun used anywhere in the spec has a one-sentence definition. An ordinary English word needs no entry.
119	- The body is a list of **requirements**. Each requirement has a short **context** (when the situation arises, who is involved, what the reader sees), one **user story** (as a person in a named role, I want one thing, so that one benefit follows), and **acceptance criteria**.
120	- The criteria are grouped into **named cases**. A case names a situation and lists two to six numbered steps. Each step carries one trigger and one response, written with the plain keywords *when*, *while*, *if*, *then*, and *shall*.
121	- Each line ends with a short code in brackets: `[INV-104]`, or `[E-6, T-12]` where several apply. The code is that rule's permanent id, and this spec line is its home. The test matrix and the architecture document cite the same code, so a maintainer can walk between all three. A reader can ignore the codes.
122	
123	A **fact** is one thing the spec says the product does. The test matrix follows the same format, defined in [`docs/test-matrix-format.md`](docs/test-matrix-format.md). Each matrix row takes one fact and states both halves of it: what it does, and what it must never do. Rows are grouped by architecture node, and the coverage table at the document's end is generated from the rows and gated against hand edits.
124	
125	The roadmap and the architecture document follow the format too. The architecture is defined in [`docs/architecture-format.md`](docs/architecture-format.md). Each part of the system stands as one node section, naming its responsibility, the facts it owns, and where it lives in the code. One shared parser reads every node section, and every check reads a node through it.
126	
127	Work enters the spec before code. A new behaviour arrives as a spec change, gets reviewed, and only then gets built. A guardrail check goes red when a shipped behaviour has no spec sentence behind it. A removed feature leaves a dated tombstone, and its history moves to `JOURNAL.md`.
128	
129	---
130	
131	## What's different
132	
133	**The gates are scripts.** Four checks decide whether a push in your project is allowed. The surface registry is the table listing the surfaces a project ships, `SURFACES.md` here. The first check reads that table both ways round: everything the registry lists is really shipped, and everything shipped is listed. The second: a change to a user-facing file carries a test. The third: every listed surface cites a spec code that exists. The fourth: no code is claimed twice and no surface is registered twice. The four are Python on the pre-push hook, mirrored in [CI](.github/workflows/gates.yml). A change that has drifted from its specification is refused. Some other frameworks enforce their specs by asking a model to check. A model having a bad day reports that it checked.
134	
135	**It can decline a gate it cannot build honestly, and records the reasoning.** One planned gate was refused. It would have gone red on a session that landed two independent pieces of work one after the other. Those two could have run side by side. The [record of that refusal](docs/prover/2026-07-18-rows386-412-414-lane-open-act.md) gives three reasons. Whether two pieces of work were independent is a senior's read, and a script sees only a diff. The evidence a correct run leaves is destroyed on purpose: a finished lane's branch is torn down when it lands. And the one signal a script could key on would fire on every lawful one-at-a-time run too. So the requirement shipped as a written discipline, held by the session and backed by no script. The rule behind that: a requirement no script can enforce stays a note, and a judgment call is never wired as an automated gate. The records are in [`docs/prover/`](docs/prover/), including the ones where the reviewer missed something and said so.
136	
137	**The rules are built for a model's failure modes.** Every claim shown for review is tagged with its source. The source is the artifact it was read from, your own recorded word, or the agent's inference. Inferences are flagged loudest ([the rule](skills/communicator/SKILL.md)). The line between what a document says and what a model filled in is invisible to a reader, and that is where the errors live. A background worker from a dead session counts as a live writer until three signals agree it stopped. Its files stop changing, its heartbeat goes stale, and it fails to answer a direct message ([`docs/worker-liveness.md`](docs/worker-liveness.md)). A decision you withdraw twice keeps its recommendation and is never raised again, because a tireless agent will go on asking ([the rule](skills/communicator/SKILL.md)).
138	
139	---
140	
141	## The rules are the product
142	
143	The rules are the part a software house would charge you for: thirty-four shared rules across the skill set, stated once in [`live-spec-base`](skills/live-spec-base/SKILL.md). They cover how a spec gets written so it stays readable. They cover when a question is worth your attention and when it is routine. They cover what a green suite does and does not prove.
144	
145	<!-- generated:count:skills-lines — scripts/gen-tree-counts.py owns the block below -->
146	
147	Written out, they and the skills carrying them run to 5,927 lines under `skills/`. Of those, 3,772 lines are the skill bodies, and the rest are the reference pages a body loads on demand. Count them yourself with `cat skills/*/SKILL.md skills/*/references/*.md | wc -l` and `cat skills/*/SKILL.md | wc -l`. A push of this repository is refused where either command disagrees with the number printed here. The body figure is what a session pays before it starts work, so it is the figure to hold down. It is held under the figure that includes the references. When it rises, every session that loads a skill pays more to begin.
148	
149	<!-- /generated:count:skills-lines -->
150	
151	You do not read them. They run.
152	
153	The relationship is the one you have with a builder. You do not need to know how; you still decide what. A good contractor does not ask the client to choose the rebar, and does not pick the kitchen either.
154	
155	The pack is opinionated. The opinions belong to one engineer, and they are not neutral industry practice. Adopting the pack adopts them.
156	
157	---
158	
159	## Staying in control
160	
161	You keep control, in a strong sense. Access to the diff was never the problem. Knowing where to look is.
162	
163	- **Nothing is decided silently.** Every default the agent picked is printed in the delivery report at the end of a change. It appears in the product's own words, marked as tweakable: *"on a phone this gallery stacks into one column."* ([the rule](skills/communicator/SKILL.md))
164	- **Routine choices are made and reported; the lane keeps moving.** Only what the documents genuinely leave open reaches you as a question.
165	- **Undo is one commit.** The change lands with its spec, matrix, and architecture together.
166	- **It cannot run away.** The gates go red and stop the push.
167	
168	Many tools offer control by asking a long list of questions up front. That is more work for you.
169	
170	---
171	
172	## What it missed
173	
174	One check hunts dead ends: a state a user can enter and cannot leave. It ran on the right screen and found nothing, because that screen did have exits. The trap was a door shown only on a first visit, with no way back to it afterwards. The check tested each state for an exit and never asked whether a page you leave can be reached again. That was the method's own fault, and it became a new rule ([`docs/lenses.md`](docs/lenses.md), INV-50).
175	
176	A test asserted that near-silent audio tracks are hidden from a view. The spec required the opposite: those tracks stay visible, with their names. The test was green for a month while the product did the wrong thing.
177	
178	And a scroll that satisfies its motion contract exactly can still feel cheap, which no rubric will catch honestly.
179	
180	> **A spec owns what a project can write down and test. Feel belongs to the owner's eye.**
181	
182	The full accounts, including the reviews that missed something and said so, live in the prover records: [`docs/prover/`](docs/prover/).
183	
184	---
185

# live-spec

**Ten working [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code) skills, plus the one shared rulebook they all load. They turn a wish spoken in passing into a specified, reviewed, tested, committed change. Scripts block the push when the documents and the code disagree.**

---

You tell your agent *"the report page needs a date filter"* and four minutes later it is written, tested, and green. The tests pass because they came from the same spec. The spec never said what happens when the date is invalid, so the agent picked some behaviour and shipped it. Nobody chose that behaviour and nobody reviewed it, and the green suite never looked at it.

That is the gap. The spec became the thing your agent builds from, and nothing checks the spec itself.

live-spec closes it. You say the sentence in passing, with nothing to file and no form. It gets classified, written into a living spec, reviewed by a formal-verification pass, covered by tests derived from that spec, coded until green, and committed with its documents in one change. A script on the pre-push hook compares the spec to the code that shipped and refuses the push when the two disagree. There is no CLI. You talk to it.

---

## Install

There are two ways in. Pick one road at step 1, then follow that road's lines wherever the steps below fork. Take the plugin road if you want to use the pack and download nothing you have to keep. Take the clone road if you want the pack's own tree on your disk, to read and to keep.

### Step 1 — get the pack onto your machine

**The plugin road.** Type two lines into Claude Code:

```
/plugin marketplace add happysasha18/live-spec
/plugin install live-spec@live-spec
```

That is the whole step. The plugin puts the entire pack tree under `~/.claude/plugins/cache/`. You do not clone this repository, now or later.

**The clone road.** Clone the repository and run its installer:

```
git clone https://github.com/happysasha18/live-spec.git
cd live-spec && ./install.sh
```

`install.sh` copies the skill folders into `~/.claude/skills/` and copies nothing else. Keep the clone. It is your copy of the pack tree, and step 3 runs a script that lives inside it.

### Step 2 — attach the pack to a project

Both roads do the same thing here. Open the project in Claude Code and say *"attach live-spec to this project"*, or *"found a new project on live-spec"* in an empty directory. The pack locates its own tree and reads yours, asks what it needs to know in plain words, and runs the whole setup walk itself — writing your first spec, and (step 3, next) wiring the push gate. You do not open any of those files yourself.

### Step 3 — the push gate

The push gate is a separate step, and it reads the documents step 2 just wrote. **The setup walk installs it too, as part of the one walk from step 2** — the checks, the config, the git hook, all of it. That is the ordinary path, and there is nothing to do here.

After that everything runs in plain words: any wish, *"status"* — where the work stands now and what is next — *"publish"*.

If you're a programmer and want to read or drive those documents yourself, the technical account starts at ["For builders"](#for-builders), below the fold. A technical wish for the pack itself is welcome — [open an Issue](https://github.com/happysasha18/live-spec/issues/new/choose); it lands in the maintainers' inbox and gets routed from there.

---

## For builders

Everything above is the whole job for a customer. What follows is for a programmer who wants to see what the setup walk does, run a piece of it by hand, wire the gate into CI, or drive the documents directly instead of through the agent.

### The technical walk-throughs

[`docs/adoption.md`](docs/adoption.md) explains the setup walk step 2 runs. The normative procedures it follows are [`adopt/ADOPT.md`](adopt/ADOPT.md) for an existing codebase and [`adopt/START.md`](adopt/START.md) for an empty directory.

### The push gate, by hand

Three things have to be true before any of it works, and each has one command that says so. `python3 --version` must print 3.9 or newer; install a newer Python if it does not. `git rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree` must print `true` in your project's root; run `git init` there if it does not. And `git rev-parse --verify origin/main` must name a commit. The tests-present check diffs your work against that ref. If the command fails, you name your own base in the config instead, two paragraphs down. It fails on a project with no remote, and on one whose default branch is named otherwise. All of this assumes Claude Code on your machine: the pack is a set of skills it loads, and step 2 happens inside it.

By hand, run one script from your project's root. It lives in the pack tree you already got in step 1, so the line you type depends on which road you took:

```
# plugin road — the tree sits in the plugin cache
bash ~/.claude/plugins/cache/*/live-spec/*/adopt/install-scaffold.sh

# clone road — the tree is the clone from step 1
bash /path/to/live-spec/adopt/install-scaffold.sh
```

It writes six files into your project's `guardrails/`: the four checks, the shared library they load, and a copy of the page that documents them. It seeds `guardrails.config.json` when your project carries none, and it never overwrites a config you already filled. It also writes `scripts/ratchet-manifest.json`, creating a `scripts/` folder if you have none. A good run prints one `vendored:` line per file and a `seeded:` line for the config. Then it prints the manual steps that remain, and ends on a line reading `{"severity": "ok", "code": "scaffold-install", ...}`.

That config then needs two things from you. Fill in your paths: the spec, the test matrix, the queue, the tests, and the surface registry. The registry is the table listing every surface the project ships. A surface is one named part a user meets: a screen, a page, a command, a public function. The queue is the dated list of what has been asked of the product and where each ask stands. This repository keeps its own in [`ROADMAP.md`](ROADMAP.md).

Three more fields in that same config decide what the checks can see. The seeded example fills them with values a fresh project rarely matches. `user_facing_globs` names the files whose change demands a test. `rendered_artifacts`, or `render_command` instead, names what the completeness check reads as your shipped output. `surface_discovery_pattern` is the expression that finds surface ids inside that output. Leave the first two as they ship and two of the four checks go red on a path that does not exist. Leave the pattern matching nothing your artifacts contain and the check passes while seeing nothing. That is the one failure that never announces itself. The setup walk in step 2 fills this config for you from what your project ships; this paragraph is for a programmer editing it by hand instead.

One field more, `base_ref`, decides what the tests-present check compares your work against when `origin/main` does not resolve. That means a project with no remote, or one whose default branch is named otherwise. Set it to your own base branch, `"base_ref": "main"`, and that check has its ground. Leave it out on such a project and the fourth line of the push gate reds with `no base ref to diff against`. [`scaffold/guardrails/README.md`](scaffold/guardrails/README.md) describes every field one at a time.

Second, empty the config's `waivers` block, so the line reads `"waivers": {}`. It ships holding one example waiver, and that example switches the completeness check off. Every run prints `WAIVED (completeness): no rendered artifact yet — declared 2026-07-10, owner <maintainer>` and exits zero. The line is loud enough. What it says is that someone else's declaration, dated before you arrived, stands where your own would go. Until you empty the block, you run on three checks instead of four.

One more step, outside the config: add these four lines to `.git/hooks/pre-push`.

```sh
python3 guardrails/check_completeness.py || exit 1
python3 guardrails/check_tests_present.py || exit 1
python3 guardrails/check_traces_to_spec.py || exit 1
python3 guardrails/check_conflicts.py || exit 1
```

Create that file if your project has none, and make it executable with `chmod +x .git/hooks/pre-push`. Run it once by hand with `sh .git/hooks/pre-push`, then `echo $?` to see the exit code. Four lines each opening `OK (` and a `0` mean the gate is live. The same four lines are in your own `guardrails/README.md`, the copy the script just vendored, on either road. Those hook lines take no arguments, so the `--base <ref>` flag the checks accept is for running one by hand. What the hook itself reads is `origin/main`, or the `base_ref` you set in the config. The setup walk writes this same hook file for you; this step is for a programmer who would rather write it themselves, or wire it into CI instead of `.git/hooks/`.

Two more installers finish the gate the adoption procedure asks for. Both run from your project's root, out of the same pack tree as before:

```
# plugin road
bash ~/.claude/plugins/cache/*/live-spec/*/adopt/install-ratchet.sh
bash ~/.claude/plugins/cache/*/live-spec/*/scripts/install-pack-hooks.sh

# clone road
bash /path/to/live-spec/adopt/install-ratchet.sh
bash /path/to/live-spec/scripts/install-pack-hooks.sh
```

The first vendors the style, redundancy, and freeze gates. It measures your documents as they stand today and writes the debt caps at those numbers. It generates `tests/test_ratchet_lock.py`, so the gate is green the day it lands and the debt can only hold or shrink from there. It ends by printing a fifth gate line for your push hook. That line belongs in the same `.git/hooks/pre-push` you just wrote, beside the four. Write it as `python3 -m pytest -q tests/test_ratchet_lock.py || exit 1`. The printed form ends `|| fail=1`, which fits a hook that collects every failure before it exits. The recipe labels it `gate r`. This repository's own hook set already gives that letter to a different check, so give yours another label if you carry that set.

The second puts the pack's own scan hooks on your machine, and this one reaches outside your project. It copies the hook files under `~/.claude/hooks/` and writes their wiring into `~/.claude/settings.json`, which every project of yours reads. Run it with `--dry-run` first: it prints every file and every line it would add, and touches nothing. Running it for real twice changes nothing, and your personal overlay files are never written by it. [`adopt/ADOPT.md`](adopt/ADOPT.md) counts both installers as part of the attach. The setup walk runs both of these for you too; they are here for a programmer setting a project up outside a live-spec session.

---

## What the spec looks like

A project under the pack keeps one document, `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, stating what the product promises today. A stranger can read a section on the first pass. The format is a requirements genre, defined in [`docs/spec-format.md`](docs/spec-format.md):

- The document opens with a **glossary**. Every domain noun used anywhere in the spec has a one-sentence definition. An ordinary English word needs no entry.
- The body is a list of **requirements**. Each requirement has a short **context** (when the situation arises, who is involved, what the reader sees), one **user story** (as a person in a named role, I want one thing, so that one benefit follows), and **acceptance criteria**.
- The criteria are grouped into **named cases**. A case names a situation and lists two to six numbered steps. Each step carries one trigger and one response, written with the plain keywords *when*, *while*, *if*, *then*, and *shall*.
- Each line ends with a short code in brackets: `[INV-104]`, or `[E-6, T-12]` where several apply. The code is that rule's permanent id, and this spec line is its home. The test matrix and the architecture document cite the same code, so a maintainer can walk between all three. A reader can ignore the codes.

A **fact** is one thing the spec says the product does. The test matrix follows the same format, defined in [`docs/test-matrix-format.md`](docs/test-matrix-format.md). Each matrix row takes one fact and states both halves of it: what it does, and what it must never do. Rows are grouped by architecture node, and the coverage table at the document's end is generated from the rows and gated against hand edits.

The roadmap and the architecture document follow the format too. The architecture is defined in [`docs/architecture-format.md`](docs/architecture-format.md). Each part of the system stands as one node section, naming its responsibility, the facts it owns, and where it lives in the code. One shared parser reads every node section, and every check reads a node through it.

Work enters the spec before code. A new behaviour arrives as a spec change, gets reviewed, and only then gets built. A guardrail check goes red when a shipped behaviour has no spec sentence behind it. A removed feature leaves a dated tombstone, and its history moves to `JOURNAL.md`.

**The gates are scripts.** Four checks decide whether a push in your project is allowed. The surface registry is the table listing the surfaces a project ships, `SURFACES.md` here. Some other frameworks enforce their specs by asking a model to check. A model having a bad day reports that it checked.

**It can decline a gate it cannot build honestly, and records the reasoning.** One planned gate was refused. It would have gone red on a session that landed two independent pieces of work one after the other. Those two could have run side by side. The evidence a correct run leaves is destroyed on purpose: a finished lane's branch is torn down when it lands. The rules are the part a software house would charge you for: thirty-four shared rules across the skill set, stated once in [`live-spec-base`](skills/live-spec-base/SKILL.md). You do not read them. They run.

The relationship is the one you have with a builder. You do not need to know how; you still decide what. A good contractor does not ask the client to choose the rebar, and does not pick the kitchen either.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""check_completeness.py — no partial or stripped artifact ships (SPEC INV-97).

The surface registry (`registry_path`) is compared against the RENDERED content both
ways: every registered surface must be present and non-empty, and — when
`surface_discovery_pattern` is set — every surface the rendered content exhibits must
be registered (the self-closing direction: you cannot drift past this by forgetting
to update a list).

Usage: python3 check_completeness.py   (config: $GUARDRAILS_CONFIG or
./guardrails.config.json; run from the host repo root)

Python 3.9 stdlib only.
"""

import os
import re
import subprocess
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)))
import gate_lib  # noqa: E402

CHECK = "completeness"
TAG = re.compile(r"<[^>]*>")


def rendered_content(config, root):
    """The content under test: `render_command`'s stdout when the host declares one,
    else every file named in `rendered_artifacts` read off disk."""
    command = config.get("render_command")
    if command:
        proc = subprocess.run(command, shell=True, cwd=root,
                              capture_output=True, text=True)
        if proc.returncode != 0:
            gate_lib.fail(CHECK, "dead-path",
                          "render_command %r exited %d: %s"
                          % (command, proc.returncode, proc.stderr.strip()[:300]),
                          "make render_command runnable from the repo root, or set it "
                          "to null and list rendered_artifacts instead")
        return proc.stdout
    artifacts = gate_lib.require_key(CHECK, config, "rendered_artifacts")
    chunks = []
    for rel in artifacts:
        full = gate_lib.require_path(CHECK, root, rel, "rendered artifact")
        chunks.append(gate_lib.read_file(full))
    return "\n".join(chunks)


def matching_lines(needle, content):
    """Lines the needle hits — as a plain substring first, else as a regex."""
    lines = [ln for ln in content.splitlines() if needle in ln]
    if lines:
        return lines, False
    try:
        pattern = re.compile(needle)
    except re.error:
        return [], False
    return [ln for ln in content.splitlines() if pattern.search(ln)], True


def line_is_empty(line, needle, is_regex):
    """Empty match content: the needle's line carries no other non-tag text."""

on:

    branches: [main]
  pull_request:

jobs:
  gates:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      TZ: Asia/Jerusalem   # gate (a) wants a today-dated prover record; "today" is the author's day, not UTC's

      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:

      - uses: actions/setup-python@v6

          python-version: "3.12"
      - name: install pytest
        run: pip install pytest
      # The external canon, pinned. Before this step existed the suite ran with no clone,
      # so every assertion that reads the externalized product-prover skipped on every CI
      # run forever, and CI claimed a green it had not earned (ROADMAP row 622 territory;
      # the same fork the emergency branch reached from the other side). The pack now
      # INSTALLS the canon rather than pretending to prove it: --ref names the exact commit
      # the pack's assertions are written against, and --expect-commit verifies the checkout
      # landed there, so a moved tag or branch cannot change what CI proves. Moving the pin
      # is a deliberate pack change; tests/test_prover_adapter_contract.py holds its shape.
      - name: install the external product-prover canon (pinned, gate b's evidence)
        run: >-
          scripts/install-external-skills.sh
          --ref 94d36454d55438951311d302fc86adba33123868
          --expect-commit 94d36454d55438951311d302fc86adba33123868
      - name: test suite (gate b, full — the reach map stays local)
        run: python3 -m pytest -q
      - name: gate a — fresh prover record (one record per push, SPEC M-6/INV-116/INV-304)
        # LIVE_SPEC_DIFF_BASE lets the script judge the inbox-only carve-out (row 269,
        # SPEC M-6/INV-112): a push whose diff is exactly one new inbox/ file owes no
        # fresh record. The same base carries the range arm, which reads the pushed delta
        # against the state the remote already holds. github.event.before is the pre-push
        # SHA on a push; on a PR it is empty and the script falls back to origin/main,
        # which the fetch-depth-0 checkout above carries.
        env:

      - name: gate o — cleanup notice (every cleanup path that ends a process says what it ended, SPEC INV-204)

        run: python3 guardrails/check-touchpoint-kind.py
      - name: gate q — waiting list (the board loses nothing — no over-cap shown set, no demotion into the void, SPEC INV-206)

      - name: gate r — authority anchor (a decision recorded as the person's names its exchange, SPEC INV-207)

      # need no separate CI step here and no ci-mirror carve-out — a suite-riding check carries no gate

        run: guardrails/check-ci-mirror.sh

        run: python3 guardrails/check-every-gate-can-fail.py

        run: python3 guardrails/check-agent-card.py
      - name: gate z — doc bound (each growable working doc within its declared bound or freshly rotated, SPEC INV-234)
        run: python3 guardrails/check-doc-bound.py
      - name: gate aa — doc findings bound (no live document above its recorded finding count, SPEC INV-301)
        # The record arm reads the record against the state the remote already holds (SPEC R302.12).
        # github.event.before is the pre-push SHA on a push; on a PR it is empty and the arm falls back
        # to origin/main, which the fetch-depth-0 checkout above carries.
        env:
          LIVE_SPEC_DIFF_BASE: ${{ github.event.before }}
        run: python3 guardrails/check-doc-findings-bound.py
      - name: gate ad — published tree counts (a count this repository publishes about its own tree is built from the tree, SPEC INV-305)
        run: python3 guardrails/check-tree-counts.py
      - name: gate ae — named checks (the registry says what each runnable file a skill body names is, SPEC INV-306)
        run: python3 guardrails/check-named-checks.py

  # After the gates pass on a real push to main, sync the standalone mirror repos from the
  # pack — the durable, cross-machine arm of the same job the local pre-push hook does (the
  # local hook covers this machine; CI covers any machine, including a browser/cloud session).
  # Auth is a per-mirror SSH deploy key held in the MIRROR_SYNC_DEPLOY_KEY secret. The job
  # skips cleanly when that secret is absent, so CI never reds for a missing key (honest
  # failure by name, SPEC INV-112). Extends the push gate (SPEC M-6) and scripts/sync-mirrors.sh
  # (SPEC INV-96).
  sync-mirrors:
    needs: gates
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v5
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
          persist-credentials: false   # the mirror push authenticates with the deploy key below, not the default token
      - name: sync standalone mirrors from the pack
        env:
          MIRROR_SYNC_DEPLOY_KEY: ${{ secrets.MIRROR_SYNC_DEPLOY_KEY }}
        run: |
          if [ -z "${MIRROR_SYNC_DEPLOY_KEY}" ]; then
            echo "MIRROR_SYNC_DEPLOY_KEY not set — skipping mirror sync (add the secret to enable the CI arm)."
            exit 0
          fi
          key_file="$(mktemp)"
          printf '%s\n' "${MIRROR_SYNC_DEPLOY_KEY}" > "$key_file"
          chmod 600 "$key_file"
          export GIT_SSH_COMMAND="ssh -i $key_file -o StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new -o IdentitiesOnly=yes"
          export MIRROR_SSH=1   # tell sync-mirrors.sh to reach the mirror over SSH, not gh/HTTPS
          git config --global user.name "live-spec mirror bot"
          git config --global user.email "mirror-bot@users.noreply.github.com"
          bash scripts/sync-mirrors.sh

=== worker-liveness three signals ===
12:- The worker touches that same checkpoint file on a fixed interval (~60 s [default]) as a bare heartbeat, whatever else its work writes. A compute-bound run — a long render, a large test pass — can write no product file for minutes; the heartbeat is what proves it still alive to the resume protocol's death check (INV-76).
31:2. Read the worker's heartbeat on its checkpoint file: a worker touches that file on a fixed interval (~60 s [default]) whatever its work writes, so a heartbeat moved within the last ~2 min [default] means a live writer even when no product file has — the case of a compute-bound run mid-computation.

# Prover record — CROSS-LINK pass + architecture lens (ROADMAP rows 386 / 412 / 414, the lane-open act)

- Pass run by: **product-prover 2.6.3** (pack version read from `VERSION` = 2.6.3, no bump this landing)
- Date: 2026-07-18
- Mode: **CROSS-LINK** — the new law INV-214 (the lane-open act) against the landed lane road it seams into (T-18, INV-49, INV-105, INV-198, INV-199, E-34, T-23, INV-2, INV-11, INV-39), plus the **architecture lens** over the parallel-lanes node, which gains its first owned file `scripts/open-lane.sh`.
- Footprint: **cross-cutting** — the act moves a shared law across PRODUCT_SPEC.md, the base rulebook, build-pipeline, the package-defaults table, the personal profile, ARCHITECTURE.md, TEST_MATRIX.md, and one new script. Full pipeline from step 1.
- Delta: three rows. **412** — the lane-open ACT (INV-214) and the honest verdict on the serial-work gate. **414** — the three-lane cap re-homed from the spec text to the settings ladder (`lanes.cap`, package default three) and the owner's value moved to his profile. **386** — the act and the discipline legs land; the live three-lane run leg is left OPEN (a field beat the orchestrator runs).
- Previous record checked (opening duty): `docs/prover/2026-07-18-batch3-push-recheck.md` and the row-420 records close folded; no unfolded row rides forward.
- Deed checks run this pass: `scripts/open-lane.sh` exercised on a real hermetic repo (claim commit on main + lane worktree cut from it; cap refusal; one-row-delta refusal; nothing-staged refusal; off-main refusal — all six by deed); the new tests red-proven by mutation 2026-07-18 (script removed → six by-deed rows red; pre-delta spec → law rows red); `tests/test_traceability.py` green (171); `tests/test_lane_branch_road.py` green (37).

## Triage

TRIAGE: PROCEED. The lane road (E-34, T-23, INV-198..201) is landed and its 372–382 matrix rows are green, so INV-214 seams into a proven structure rather than a moving one. The act is a real performable thing (the script runs and its guards fire by deed), so the row's central claim is verified rather than asserted.

## The two things row 412 owed, and how each was met

**1. The lane-open ACT — built, and it is a thing a session DOES.** The gap 412 named is exact: the law GRANTS lanes (T-18) and the branch road gives the grant a mechanism (E-34, T-23), but no step ever OPENED one, so a session had nothing to perform and took the single-file road every time. INV-214 makes opening a lane a named, performable act with a home in the method (base-rulebook rule 7's lanes sub-rules + build-pipeline's Trains section) and a performable form, `scripts/open-lane.sh`. The act commits the row→in-work flip on main under the pen [INV-198, T-23, INV-2], cuts `lane/<row>-<slug>` from that claim commit into its own worktree [E-34], and hands the lane to a worker whose brief names the branch (the Agent tool's `isolation: "worktree"` option carries no gate and works today). The script's guards are proven by deed on a real repo, not trusted from its prose: the claim lands on main (so INV-2's ancestry can read it), the claim commit carries only the queue file (INV-39's one-row delta), the fence is re-checked where armed (INV-11), and the cap is enforced. This is the fix for "a law with no machine is a wish".

**2. The gate that reds serial independent work — DECIDED as a DISCIPLINE, with the reasoning, and NOT shipped as a hollow gate.** This is the hard part, and the honest verdict is that it cannot be a sound mechanical gate. Three reasons, each concrete:

  - **Independence is a senior judgment, not a diff.** Deciding that two rows were independent and *should* have rolled in parallel IS the independence graph [INV-49] — an edge wherever two rows share a surface, a spec section, a skill file, or a doc region, computed from a prediction of each row's write-set. That prediction is a read, not a mechanical fact a gate can recompute.
  - **The evidence a right run would leave is destroyed by design.** A lane branch is torn down at its landing [T-23, INV-199]. So at any push-gate moment `git branch --list 'lane/*'` shows the currently-open lanes, never whether lanes *were* used for already-landed rows. The reflog is local and gc-prunable, so no durable push-time signal survives to key a gate on.
  - **The one mechanical signal on offer reds every lawful serial movement.** The candidate "≥2 rows landed with no `lane/*` branch cut → red" fires on a dependency chain, a shared surface, and a pair of tiny rows (INV-49: "tiny rows ride serial"), all of which SHOULD be serial. Adding a "unless a reason is recorded" escape makes the gate quiet only when a reason exists — which reduces it to a prose scan that still cannot judge whether the recorded reason is *correct*, since that judgment is the independence read again.

  So the check stays a **discipline** the session holds: when the graph shows two or more independent runnable rows with lanes free under the cap, the session performs the act, and going single-file then is a recorded "serial by the graph" board line naming which standing reason holds. This is row 420's own audit rule applied to itself — a taste/judgment call is never a gate — and the meta-gate w would red a hollow gate that cannot truly fire, so shipping one would be caught anyway. No new gate letter is minted, no entry is added to `gate-red-proofs.json`, and the meta-gate's coverage is unchanged. The one mechanical guard the act genuinely carries — the cap refusal — is deterministic (a count of open `lane/*` branches against the profile cap) and IS built and tested by deed.

## Row 414 — the cap re-homed to the settings ladder

The number "three" was one person's setting wearing a law's clothes: every host that vendors the pack inherited the owner's budget. The value moves to the settings ladder [E-13]: a `lanes.cap` row in the package-defaults table (default three), the owner's 2026-07-06 value recorded as a `lanes.cap: 3` line in his personal profile (naming that exchange), and every spec/skill sentence that hardcoded "three" now reads "the profile-declared lane cap (`lanes.cap`, package default three)". A host with no profile line inherits the sensible default of three. The act reads this cap and refuses a lane past it.

**A deliberate simplification, named:** row 414's original text imagined an "adoption gate that reds a host whose profile answers nothing". That is superseded by the sensible-default rule — every setting on the ladder has a package default, and `lanes.cap` defaults to three, so a host with no line is not a red, it is a host on the default. Reding a missing line would contradict the ladder's own law. No adoption gate is built; the default covers the silent host.

## Findings

- **F1 (folded).** One-home check: the cap value must not live in two places. Folded — the value's normative home is the package-defaults table (default) plus the profile (the owner's value); every other mention (spec 521/535/587, T-18 index, base rule 7, build-pipeline Trains) now *references* `lanes.cap` rather than restating the number. Verified by grep: no surviving "three build lanes" / "a fourth lane" hardcoding outside the two homes and the historical prose.
- **F2 (folded).** Traceability: `test_parallel_lanes_law` pinned the old "At most three build lanes" / "a fourth lane opens" literals. Under the docs-travel-with-a-spec-backed-literal tripwire [INV-104] the test's needles were updated to the de-hardcoded wording in the same landing. Suite green.
- **R1 (recommendation, queued as the row's own OPEN leg).** The live three-lane run in one window is row 386/412's own worked instance and is left OPEN by design — it is a field beat the orchestrator runs, reported with what it cost. Not claimed done here.
- **R2 (recommendation, pre-existing, not this delta's).** The config-health check that would red a `lane/*` branch with no open row and a primary tree off main remains [target] (INV-198/199), riding row 386's build half. Out of this landing's scope; the prover's station is its net meanwhile [INV-150].

## Architecture lens

The parallel-lanes node previously owned no file of its own — its law lived inside the two skills that perform it. `scripts/open-lane.sh` is the node's first owned file, pinned in the node row. INV-214 is added to the node's owned-anchor list (owned once, checked by `test_traceability.py::test_architecture_owns_every_anchor_once`, green). The seam "lane set → the pipeline's steps" is unchanged; the act is the step that reads the graph's verdict. No new node, no new seam.

## Verdict

PROCEED. The act is real and proven by deed; the serial-work check is honestly recorded as a discipline with its reasoning rather than shipped as a hollow gate; the cap is re-homed to the ladder with a sensible default; the live three-lane run is left OPEN. No blocking finding.

# live-spec — the ideas in five minutes

This page is for a developer who has read the README and wants the ideas before opening any skill
file. Normative rules live in `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` and the skill files; this page explains and points.

## The living spec is the product's source of truth

A project running under the pack keeps one document, `PRODUCT_SPEC.md`, stating what the product
promises today. That project is called the host, and the pack's own repository is a host too.
The document opens with a glossary that defines every domain noun, then a body of
requirements: each carries a short context (when the situation arises, who is involved, what the
reader sees), one user story, and acceptance criteria grouped into named cases. Short codes such as `[INV-104]` or
`[E-6, T-12]` trail at line ends as anchors for the machine; a reader can ignore them. A generated code-to-location table
closes the document. The pack's own spec is the reference shape; its version lives in `VERSION`.

The spec is living in a precise sense. Work enters it before code: a new behaviour arrives as a spec
delta, gets reviewed, and only then gets built. Shipped behaviour traces back to it: a guardrail
check goes red when a user-facing behaviour has no spec sentence behind it. And it stays current:
a removed feature leaves a dated tombstone, and history moves to `JOURNAL.md`.

## The pipeline — a wish becomes shipped, tested work

A wish is a request in plain words, thrown at any moment. It becomes one row in the queue,
`ROADMAP.md`, the moment it is spoken (SPEC E-2). Intake names its **door** aloud — the intake
classification that places a wish at one entry point, decided before any code is written and
independent of the wish's size: feature, bug, refactor, docs-only, skip. Fixed tripwires decide,
so a casual ask that creates a new surface still enters as a feature (SPEC T-12). A feature walks
nine stations in order.

1. **Spec** — `spec-author` writes the delta: entities, states, transitions, invariants, regression
   fences on touched live surfaces, a sweep of the standard facets (the viewport bands, touch,
   the empty and error states, keyboard reach), non-goals, one success measure.
2. **Prove** — `product-prover` reviews the grown spec; findings are recorded and folded.
3. **Architecture** — `ARCHITECTURE.md` maps named nodes, each owning spec facts, pinned to real
   `file:line`. The document also owes a runtime view (each promised flow walked node by node, with
   a fallback at every failure point, SPEC INV-74) and a placement view saying where every node
   runs (SPEC INV-75).
4. **Prove the architecture** — the prover again, with an architecture lens: every fact owned,
   every node backed by the spec, every seam named, both views present.
5. **Test matrix** — `test-author` derives `TEST_MATRIX.md`, one block per node, one row per fact;

Full stumble list from reading `/private/tmp/live-spec-readme2/wt/README.md` top to bottom and clicking through the files it points at.

**1. MINOR — Narrative cold open before any mechanics**
Section: intro (before "## Install"). Quote: *"You tell your agent 'the report page needs a date filter' and four minutes later it is written, tested, and green."* A four-sentence anecdote before the doc gets to what the tool actually does. Short enough that I kept reading, but it's the customer-pitch voice up front, not engineer voice.

**2. MINOR — Alarming framing that gets walked back later**
Section: intro. Quote: *"There is no CLI. You talk to it."* Read cold, this says "chatbot toy, not automatable." It's only in "For builders" that you learn there are real scripts, a config schema, and CI wiring. The claim is technically true (no interactive CLI binary) but the phrasing cost me a moment of "why am I looking at this."

**3. MINOR — Padded metaphor before the two commands that matter**
Section: "## Install." Quote: *"Pick one road at step 1, then follow that road's lines wherever the steps below fork."* The "roads" conceit runs the whole Install section. The actual technical content is two shell snippets; the metaphor is filler around them.

**4. MINOR — The "skip to the technical part" signpost comes after the part I'd want to skip**
Section: "### Step 3 — the push gate" (end). Quote: *"the technical account starts at ['For builders'](#for-builders), below the fold."* This is the exact signpost I wanted — but it only appears after I've already read the full customer-facing Install narrative (lines 1–48). This is the (b) case: the doc doesn't tell me "this isn't for you" until after I've read it.

**5. MINOR — Reference example doesn't match the "by hand" instructions when you check it**
Section: "### The push gate, by hand." Quote: *"It writes six files into your project's `guardrails/`: the four checks, the shared library they load, and a copy of the page that documents them."* This repo's own `guardrails/` has ~90 files, none named `check_completeness.py` / `check_tests_present.py` / `check_traces_to_spec.py` / `check_conflicts.py`. Those four actually live under `scaffold/guardrails/` (the template copied into a *host* project — this repo dogfoods a much larger, differently-named internal gate set instead). True once you find it, but cross-checking the README against its own repo sent me down a side path.

**6. BLOCKING — The exact silent-failure footgun the README warns about is live in its own config**
Section: "### The push gate, by hand." Quote: *"Leave the pattern matching nothing your artifacts contain and the check passes while seeing nothing. That is the one failure that never announces itself."* I checked this repo's own `guardrails.config.json`: `surface_discovery_pattern` is still `"<section id=\"([^\"]+)\""`, `render_command` is `null`, and `rendered_artifacts` is `["README.md", "OVERVIEW.md"]` — plain markdown, containing zero literal `<section id="` tags anywhere. I read `scaffold/guardrails/check_completeness.py`: when `render_command` is unset it reads the raw files, runs `re.findall(discovery, content)`, and if that returns nothing the reverse-direction check (`rendered-but-unregistered`) always passes trivially — it can never fire. I confirmed this is the unmodified value from `scaffold/guardrails/guardrails.config.example.json`, i.e. nobody customized it for this repo. So the maintainer's own flagship self-hosted example ships with half of one of its "four checks that decide whether a push is allowed" permanently inert, in precisely the failure mode the README calls out two paragraphs earlier as the one that "never announces itself." That's the kind of thing that makes me stop trusting the rest of the rigor claims without independently re-verifying them.

**7. MINOR — "mirrored in CI" undersells the CI file by an order of magnitude**
Section: "## What's different." Quote: *"The four are Python on the pre-push hook, mirrored in [CI](.github/workflows/gates.yml)."* Opening that file shows not four mirrored checks but roughly 25 named gates (a, b, d, e, f, g, h, i, j, l, n, o, p, q, r, s, t, u, w, x, y, z, aa, ad, ae) covering things never mentioned in the README (Cyrillic-text linting, browser-kill hygiene, mirror-repo sync, doc-size ratchets…). "The four" turn out to be one step, labeled `gate h`, buried in that list. Not false, but the sentence implies a simple 1:1 mirror and the link reveals a much bigger, undocumented system.

**8. MINOR — Scale of the living documents isn't signaled anywhere**
Section: "## What the spec looks like." Quote: *"A stranger can read a section on the first pass."* True of a section, but `PRODUCT_SPEC.md` is 703KB, `TEST_MATRIX.md` 484KB, `ROADMAP.md` 292KB, `JOURNAL.md` 373KB in this repo. The README never signals that adopting this seriously means carrying documents at this scale; the calm, single-example tone undersells the operational weight.

---

**What worked well, for balance:** the doc's self-checkable claims mostly held up under scrutiny — the "5,927 / 3,772 lines" self-count matched exactly (`cat skills/*/SKILL.md skills/*/references/*.md | wc -l`), "thirty-four shared rules" matched the skill file, the worker-liveness three-signal description matched `docs/worker-liveness.md` verbatim in substance, the prover-refusal record at `docs/prover/2026-07-18-rows386-412-414-lane-open-act.md` matched the README's summary of it closely and in more honest detail than the README even claims, and the "gate r" label collision the README warns about (line 108) is real and verifiable in `.github/workflows/gates.yml` vs `adopt/install-ratchet.sh`. Every linked file existed and said roughly what was implied, except for the config drift in #6.

**(a) Fast path to technical substance:** Mostly yes. "For builders" is a real, well-marked jump point with genuine schema/command/script detail beneath it (config fields, hook wiring, exact CLI invocations) — better than most READMEs in this genre. The cost is getting there: ~48 lines of customer narrative first.

**(b) Wastes time before saying "not for you":** Yes, once (stumble #4), and mildly.

**Final count: 1 blocking, 7 minor.**
